Weather

Air and water along the way

Night sky

Stargazing at sea

Away from city lights the sky gets very dark. The moon was full on Dec 24, so each evening starts dark and the moon rises later every night.

What to look for

Saturn Evening, high in the south
A steady, pale-gold point high in the south after sunset. It sets around 1 am. You need a telescope to see the rings.
Jupiter and Regulus Rises about 10 pm in the east
The brightest thing in the late-night sky, sitting about 3.5° (two finger-widths) from Regulus, the heart of Leo. Brace binoculars on the rail and look for up to four moons in a line.
Mars Rises about 11 pm
Orange-red, about 10° from Jupiter. It's brightening toward opposition in February 2027.
Venus Before dawn, low in the southeast
The 'morning star', far brighter than anything else in the sky. It rises around 4 am.
Canopus Around midnight, low in the south
The second-brightest star in the night sky. It never rises in Portland and barely clears San Diego's horizon, but off Mexico it climbs to about 15°.
Orion and Sirius Evening onward, east to south
Orion is high by midnight; follow his belt down-left to Sirius, the brightest star.
Polaris drops Due north, all night
Polaris sits at an altitude equal to your latitude: about 32° in San Diego and about 23° off Mazatlán. A fist at arm's length is roughly 10°.
Southern Cross (long shot) Just before dawn, due south
On Dec 29–30 its top star, Gacrux, reaches about 10° in twilight. The rest of the cross stays too low to see.
Green flash The moment the sun sets
A clear sea horizon is the best place to catch a brief green flash on the sun's last sliver. Look right at the last moment, not before.
Glowing wake On a dark night, looking down
Bioluminescent plankton can sparkle blue-green in the ship's wake. Look straight down from an open deck aft or along the side.

How to stargaze from the ship

  • Find the darkest open deck you can, often forward or aft on the upper decks, away from pool lights.
  • Give your eyes 15–20 minutes. Turn your phone to red night mode (Sky Guide has one) and dim the screen.
  • Your phone's GPS works with no signal, so Sky Guide places the stars correctly at sea. Its support pages say it needs no internet.
  • At 12× magnification the view shakes on a moving ship. Brace your elbows on the rail, or lean against a wall.

Apps

Sky Guide
Works fully offline. Point it at the sky to name stars and planets; it also shows stars below the horizon.
Stellarium Mobile
Free, with a deeper catalog. Good as a backup and for planning by setting any date and place.
SkyView Lite
Free and the simplest point-and-identify app.

Why the Sea of Cortez exists

The water you cross on Dec 28 and Dec 31 is a young sea, opened by plate tectonics.

How a diesel-electric ship moves

Estimates, not Holland America figures. The model assumes the pods reach their 28 MW at the 22.2-knot maximum, propulsion power rising with speed cubed, an 8.5 MW hotel load, about 190 g of fuel per kWh, generators kept under 85% load, and 2,650 guests.

Scale

How big is 300 meters?

The ship

24 facts about Koningsdam

  1. The engines never turn a propeller. Four diesel generators feed one electrical grid that powers both the propulsion motors and the hotel: lights, galleys, air conditioning.
  2. There is no conventional rudder. Each Azipod is an electric motor in a pod under the hull that rotates 360°, so the ship steers by pointing its thrust.
  3. Each MaK 12V43C has 12 cylinders with a 43 cm bore and a 61 cm stroke. One cylinder sweeps about 89 liters, so a single cylinder is about 44 times a typical 2.0-liter car engine.
  4. Total generating power is 50.4 MW, about 67,600 hp, or roughly 66 Tesla Model S Plaids flat out.
  5. Propulsion power rises with the cube of speed. Going from 18 to 22 knots needs about 83% more propulsion power.
  6. Its hull, redesigned bulbous bow and local cooling let it use about 20% less power than Nieuw Amsterdam while carrying about 20% more guests.
  7. Fincantieri built it at Marghera in Venice. It was the yard's 15th ship for Holland America.
  8. Steel was cut on Feb 4, 2014. The keel was laid on Aug 22, 2014 with a 680-ton block. Delivery was March 31, 2016 and the maiden voyage followed on April 8.
  9. For luck, two gold coins showing King Willem-Alexander were welded into the hull at a coin ceremony in February 2015.
  10. Queen Máxima of the Netherlands christened the ship in Rotterdam on May 20, 2016.
14 more facts
  1. Koningsdam means King's dam. The name honors Willem-Alexander, the first Dutch king in more than a century.
  2. At delivery it was the largest ship Holland America had ever commissioned. Royal Caribbean's Icon class is about 2.5 times its gross tonnage.
  3. It is about 30 m longer than Titanic and has more than twice Titanic's enclosed volume.
  4. Six tenders built by Hatecke ferry guests ashore at anchor ports. One of them takes you into Cabo.
  5. The whole design is music-themed, down to the deck names: Beethoven, Gershwin, Schubert.
  6. World Stage is a two-deck theater seating 667, with a 270° wall of LED screens.
  7. Lincoln Center Stage seats 330 for chamber music. Later in the evening the same room becomes B.B. King's Blues Club.
  8. BLEND by Chateau Ste. Michelle was the first wine-blending venue at sea. Ten guests at a time blend their own bottle from barrels.
  9. The Lido pool sits under a magrodome, a retractable glass roof, so it works in any weather.
  10. The ship's IT systems were supplied by Lufthansa Systems.
  11. It was designed to meet Safe Return to Port rules: redundant engine rooms and systems so it can sail home on its own after a fire or flooding in one zone.
  12. The Crow's Nest on Deck 12 forward has about 270° of view. It is the best whale-watching seat on the ship.
  13. Cabins have both U.S. 110 V and European 220 V outlets. Surge protectors are banned, so bring a plain multi-USB charger.
  14. In December 2021, a crew COVID outbreak stopped guests from going ashore in Puerto Vallarta. You'll get the day your predecessors missed.
The line

Holland America Line · 21 facts

  1. Founded April 18, 1873 in Rotterdam as the Nederlandsch-Amerikaansche Stoomvaart Maatschappij, the Netherlands-America Steamship Company. The line still marks April 18.
  2. The first Rotterdam sailed from the Netherlands to New York in 1872 under the predecessor firm Plate, Reuchlin & Co.
  3. The public called it Holland America Line for years before the name became official in 1896.
  4. Its ships carried hundreds of thousands of European emigrants to America: people westbound, cargo eastbound.
  5. Regular Rotterdam–North America passenger service ended in 1971. The line ran its first standalone Atlantic crossing in 40 years in 2011.
  6. When Germany invaded in 1940, the company moved its seat to Curaçao. Nieuw Amsterdam (1938) then carried hundreds of thousands of Allied troops.
  7. Since the 1890s nearly every ship name ends in -dam, after Dutch places built around dams: Rotterdam, Amsterdam, Edam, Schiedam.
  8. The four Vista-class ships are named for the compass: Oosterdam, Westerdam, Noordam and Zuiderdam.
  9. The 2021 flagship is the seventh ship named Rotterdam. Rotterdam V (1959) is now a hotel in Rotterdam harbor.
  10. Part of Carnival Corporation since 1989, with headquarters in Seattle.
11 more facts
  1. The fleet is 11 mid-size ships of about 61,000–100,000 GT. P&O's Arcadia joins in 2029.
  2. In April 2026 the line announced Holland America Evolution: more than $500 million to refit six ships, starting with Oosterdam in fall 2027.
  3. It sails to nearly 400 ports in 114 countries.
  4. It has sailed Alaska for more than 75 years, longer than any other line.
  5. Its private island in the Bahamas, Half Moon Cay, is now RelaxAway, Half Moon Cay, shared with Carnival.
  6. The line turned 150 in 2023.
  7. Members of the Dutch royal family have christened its ships many times.
  8. Much of the crew is Indonesian and Filipino. The crew show, if your sailing has one, is often the best night of the week.
  9. In 1912, ice warnings from its ship Noordam were relayed to Titanic.
  10. Music partners aboard include B.B. King's, Billboard, Lincoln Center and Rolling Stone.
  11. It has no new ships on order. It is refitting its fleet and taking over Arcadia instead.

Phones at sea

  • Keep phones in airplane mode at sea. The ship's maritime cell network roams at high rates, even for texts.
  • The Navigator app runs on the ship's network without a paid Wi-Fi plan: daily program, deck plans and your account.
  • GPS still works in airplane mode, so offline maps and Sky Guide know where you are.
  • In port, check whether your phone plan includes Mexico, or set up a Mexico eSIM before you go.

San Diego

Where California began, now a Navy town, biotech hub and the Zoo's home.

Sat Dec 26 · sail 5 pm · Sat Jan 2 · arrive 7 amB Street Pier or Broadway PierUTC−8
Dec 26

Embarkation day

  • Terminal: B Street Pier (1140 N. Harbor Dr.) or the neighboring Broadway Pier. Your Holland America documents say which.
  • From LA it's about 120 miles, 2–2.5 hours. Aim to arrive within your check-in window; all aboard is about an hour before the 5 pm sailing.
  • Port-run parking lots sit beside the terminal. Reserve ahead if you can and check current rates.
  • Drop people and bags at the curb first, then park. Porters take checked bags; about $2 a bag is customary.
  • Keep passports, medications, swimsuits and chargers in your carry-on. Checked bags may not reach the cabin until evening.
Jan 2

Getting off the ship

  • Self-assist walk-off: carry all your own bags and leave first, usually from about 7:30 am.
  • Tagged luggage: put bags out the night before, leave later in the morning by your assigned group, and collect them in the terminal.
  • Customs (CBP) is quick for U.S. citizens. Have passports ready.
  • The Zoo is about 2.5 miles from the pier, roughly 10 minutes by car. Keep luggage out of sight in the trunk anywhere you park.

Overview

What it's known for

San Diego is California's second-largest city, with about 1.39 million people, and the county holds about 3.3 million. It sits beside Tijuana and the San Ysidro crossing, one of the busiest land border crossings in the world.

Its economy runs on the Navy, life sciences, telecom and tourism. You'll see it twice: sailing out past Point Loma on Dec 26, and coming home to a full Zoo day on Jan 2.

Fun facts

22 things to know about San Diego

  1. The Kumeyaay have lived here for more than 10,000 years, on both sides of today's border.
  2. Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo sailed into the bay on Sept 28, 1542, the first European on the U.S. West Coast. Cabrillo National Monument stands on Point Loma, which you sail past.
  3. Sebastián Vizcaíno named it San Diego in 1602.
  4. Mission San Diego de Alcalá, founded July 16, 1769 by Junípero Serra, was the first of California's 21 missions.
  5. It was Mexican from 1821 and American from 1848. The city incorporated in 1850.
  6. Balboa Park covers about 1,200 acres with 17 museums. It hosted the 1915 Panama-California Exposition.
  7. Parking in Balboa Park stopped being free on Jan 5, 2026, after more than a century.
  8. The Hotel del Coronado (1888) is the hotel in Some Like It Hot.
  9. USS Midway served from 1945 to 1992, the longest-serving U.S. carrier of the 20th century. It's been a museum beside the cruise terminal since 2004.
  10. Naval Base San Diego is home port for much of the Pacific Fleet, one of the largest concentrations of military power anywhere.
12 more facts
  1. Qualcomm was founded here in 1985. Its CDMA work underpins modern cellular networks.
  2. Comic-Con began here in 1970.
  3. The Torrey pine, the rarest native pine in the U.S., grows wild only here and on Santa Rosa Island.
  4. Rubio's (1983) popularized the fish taco in the U.S.
  5. The California burrito, carne asada with fries inside, is a San Diego invention.
  6. La Jolla Cove is an ecological reserve with garibaldi, the bright-orange state marine fish, and a big sea-lion colony.
  7. Children's Pool beach in La Jolla closes Dec 15 – May 15 for harbor-seal pupping.
  8. Scripps Institution of Oceanography runs the Birch Aquarium.
  9. Me at the zoo, the first YouTube video ever (2005), was filmed in front of the San Diego Zoo's elephants.
  10. Dr. Seuss lived in La Jolla, and UC San Diego's Geisel Library is named for him.
  11. California condors recovered from as few as 22 birds, with the Zoo's help.
  12. Gray whales pass Point Loma from December to April, so look for blows as you sail out.

The pandas

  • Yun Chuan (male, born 2019) and Xin Bao (female, born 2020) arrived in June 2024 and debuted on Aug 8, 2024 at Denny Sanford Panda Ridge, four times larger than the old habitat.
  • Yun Chuan's mother, Zhen Zhen, was born at this zoo in 2007; his grandmother was Bai Yun. He's a second-generation San Diego panda.
  • Tell them apart: Yun Chuan has a long, slightly pointed nose and is laid back. Xin Bao has a round face and big ears, and loves to climb.
  • They live in neighboring habitats and swap regularly. Together they eat about 50,000 lb of bamboo a year.
  • They're on a 10-year loan, the only giant pandas on the West Coast. No cub had been announced as of September 2026.

Tickets, hours, parking

  • Hours: 9 am – 5 pm daily. Jungle Bells holiday lights (Dec 18, 2026 – Jan 3, 2027) may keep it open later.
  • Tickets: 1-Day Pass $78 adult / $68 child, including the Guided Bus Tour and the Skyfari aerial tram. Buy online ahead.
  • Parking: $16 per vehicle per day since Jan 5, 2026, first come first served. The Inspiration Point lot, a mile south, has a shuttle.
  • Animals are most active in the first two hours after opening.
  1. Dr. Harry Wegeforth founded it in 1916 after hearing a lion left over from the 1915 Exposition roar.
  2. Admission in 1923 was 10¢.
  3. It pioneered barless, moated exhibits.
  4. The first YouTube video was filmed in front of its elephants.
  5. The Frozen Zoo, started in 1975, stores living cells from more than 1,000 species. It has helped clone Przewalski's horses and black-footed ferrets.
  6. Six panda cubs were born here between 1996 and 2019.
  7. The pandas traveled about 7,000 miles from Sichuan.
  8. Panda Ridge's plantings mimic the forests of Sichuan, Gansu and Shaanxi.
  9. Its conservation work has helped bring back more than 44 endangered species.
  10. The Skyfari has run since 1969.
10 more Zoo facts
  1. The Wild Animal Park, now the Safari Park, opened in 1972, 35 miles north.
  2. More than 700,000 plants grow here, some as animal food.
  3. Its kids' TV channel plays in children's hospitals in 14 countries.
  4. The Zoo leases its land from the city, so the City Council had to amend the lease before it could charge for parking.
  5. Condors recovered from as few as 22 birds, with help from its breeding program.
  6. Koalas sleep 18–22 hours a day, so see them when they're awake if you can.
  7. It's accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums.
  8. It reaches more than 1 billion people a year in 170 countries, by its own count.
  9. Bai Yun and Gao Gao, the earlier panda pair, lived here from 1996 to 2019.
  10. In 2024, Yun Chuan and Xin Bao were the first pandas to enter the U.S. in 21 years.

Safari Park instead?

The Safari Park (15500 San Pasqual Valley Rd., Escondido) is 35 miles from the Zoo, 45–60 minutes. It's open 9–5 with $20 parking: giraffes, rhinos and antelope in open savanna. It sits on I-15, so you could keep going to LA afterward. You can't do both parks well in one day, so pick the Zoo for the pandas.

More San Diego

Other good stops on Jan 2

La Jolla Cove
Sea lions and seals from the seawall (Children's Pool is closed for pupping). The water is about 57–60°F, so snorkeling for garibaldi needs a rented 5–7 mm wetsuit from a La Jolla Shores shop.
Birch Aquarium
Scripps' aquarium, about 1.5–2 hours.
Torrey Pines Reserve
Clifftop trails above the beach. Watch for gray whales offshore.
USS Midway Museum
Next to the cruise terminal. Allow 2–3 hours; the engineering spaces are the draw.
Coast north
Encinitas, Carlsbad, the Oceanside Pier, then Laguna Beach tide pools at low tide.
Food
Oscar's or Mariscos German for fish tacos; Lolita's or Lucha Libre for a California burrito; George's at the Cove for the view.

Banderas Bay

By the numbers

At a glance

291,839people in the municipality2020 census; 224,166 in the city
8.35 Mpeople in Jalisco2020 census

Overview

What it's known for

Puerto Vallarta wraps around Banderas Bay, about 42 by 32 km, with the jungle-covered Sierra Madre rising straight behind it. From north to south: Marina Vallarta and the Hotel Zone, where you dock; El Centro with the Malecón and the crowned church; the Zona Romántica and Los Muertos Beach; then the cliff road south to Mismaloya and Boca de Tomatlán, where boats and trails reach beaches with no road at all.

North across the Ameca River is the state of Nayarit and the Riviera Nayarit: Bucerías, Sayulita and Punta de Mita. The bay is a humpback whale nursery from December to March, so you arrive at the start of the season.

Humpback whalesLos ArcosIslas MarietasMalecón sculpturesThe Night of the IguanaTequila & raicillaHuichol beadworkPescado embaradoZona RománticaCanopy tours
History

From first peoples to now

Tap an era to expand it.

~850–1350Aztatlán coast

Aztatlán-culture villages trade along the coast. The Wixárika and Cora peoples hold the Sierra behind the bay.

1525Spanish arrival

Francisco Cortés de San Buenaventura's expedition reaches the bay. Tradition says 'Banderas' (flags) refers to the banners of the Indigenous warriors who met them.

1565–1815Galleons and pirates

Manila galleons pass offshore on their way to Acapulco. Pirates use the bay to water and hide.

1851Las Peñas

A small port is founded to land salt and supplies for the silver mines inland.

1918Puerto Vallarta

The village becomes a municipality named for Governor Ignacio L. Vallarta.

1963Hollywood

The Night of the Iguana films at Mismaloya, and the press covering Burton and Taylor puts the town on the map.

1968–1970City and airport

Official city status, then an international airport and highway links.

1995The crown falls

An earthquake topples the church crown. A replacement goes up soon after.

2016Hidden Beach limits

The Marietas reopen with a 116-a-day cap and two closed days a week.

Fun facts

22 things to know about Puerto Vallarta

  1. It was founded on Dec 12, 1851, the feast of the Virgin of Guadalupe, as Las Peñas de Santa María de Guadalupe, by Guadalupe Sánchez Torres.
  2. It began as a landing for salt and supplies bound for the silver mines at San Sebastián and Cuale up in the Sierra.
  3. It is named for Ignacio L. Vallarta, a 19th-century governor of Jalisco.
  4. It became a city only in 1968. The international airport followed around 1970.
  5. The Night of the Iguana (filmed 1963 at Mismaloya) brought John Huston, Richard Burton, Ava Gardner and Deborah Kerr. Elizabeth Taylor came too, and the world's press followed her.
  6. Burton and Taylor joined their houses in Gringo Gulch with a pink 'love bridge' over the street. The complex is Casa Kimberley.
  7. The Nayarit side of the bay keeps Jalisco's clock rather than its own state's, so the whole bay shares one time.
  8. The city says it gets more than 5 million visitors a year.
  9. The bronze Caballito de Mar (seahorse rider, 1976) is the Malecón's icon. Sergio Bustamante's In Search of Reason, two figures climbing a ladder into the sky, is the one everyone photographs.
  10. The church of Our Lady of Guadalupe wears a crown modeled on Empress Carlota's. An earthquake toppled it in 1995 and it was replaced.
12 more facts
  1. Humpbacks mate and calve in the bay from December to March. Male song carries for miles underwater; snorkelers sometimes hear it.
  2. The Islas Marietas are a national park and UNESCO biosphere reserve with blue-footed boobies.
  3. Hidden Beach on the Marietas has been capped at 116 visitors a day since it reopened in 2016, and is closed Mondays and Tuesdays. Your visit is a Tuesday.
  4. Local legend says early-1900s military target practice helped blast the Hidden Beach crater. It is often repeated and hard to verify.
  5. Los Arcos are granite arches and tunnels in a protected marine park 15–20 minutes south by boat.
  6. Tequila must be made from blue Weber agave, which takes about 6–8 years to mature, and only in Jalisco and parts of four other states.
  7. Raicilla is the coast's mezcal-like 'moonshine', made in the mountains behind the bay. It now has its own protected designation of origin.
  8. Mariachi (2011) and charrería, Mexican rodeo (2016), are both UNESCO-listed traditions from Jalisco.
  9. Wixárika (Huichol) yarn paintings and beadwork are sold downtown. Buy from cooperatives or galleries that name the artist.
  10. Olive ridley sea turtles nest on Vallarta's beaches.
  11. Jalisco is Mexico's #4 state economy and one of its tech hubs. Guadalajara's electronics plants shipped nearly $53 billion of computer equipment in 2025.
  12. The Marina Vallarta cruise terminal is about 3 miles north of the Malecón, so you'll want a cab or Uber into town.
Practical

Know before you go ashore

Getting ashore

  • The terminal is at Marina Vallarta, 3–3.4 miles north of the Malecón. It's too far to walk in the heat.
  • Uber picks up at the gate on Av. Francisco Medina Ascencio. Yellow taxis outside the gate (about 80–100 MXN) are cheaper than the cabs inside it. The ride takes 15–20 minutes.
  • The 'Centro' bus costs about 10 pesos if you want the local experience.
  • Boca de Tomatlán is about 40–45 minutes south by taxi. Pangas from there go to Los Arcos, Colomitos, Las Ánimas and Yelapa.

Snorkeling & animals

  • Top spot: Los Arcos marine park, with reef fish, morays and sometimes rays or turtles. Visibility is about 5–15 m.
  • Marietas tours snorkel the outer reefs. On a Tuesday there is no Hidden Beach landing, so don't pay a premium for it.
  • Bring your own masks for fit and hygiene. Skip fins: they're bulky and tours supply them.
  • Use mineral (zinc oxide) sunscreen or a rash guard. Protected parks require biodegradable sunscreen.

Safety

  • Jalisco is U.S. Level 3 (reconsider travel) for terrorism, crime and kidnapping, but the advisory places no restrictions on travel in Puerto Vallarta or neighboring Riviera Nayarit.
  • Jalisco is home base for the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG). When the army killed its leader, El Mencho, on Feb 22, 2026, cartel members set burning-vehicle roadblocks across the state for several hours. Smoke rose over Puerto Vallarta, Canada told its citizens there to shelter in place, and some flights were canceled. Flights were scheduled to run normally the next day.
  • Use Uber or dispatched taxis rather than street hails. The Mexico page has a short list of what to do if something flares up while you're ashore.

Overview

What it's known for

Mazatlán sits on a peninsula where the Gulf of California meets the Pacific, across from the tip of Baja. It is a working city as much as a resort: Mexico's biggest Pacific fishing port, home of the Pacífico brewery, and lined by a seafront Malecón about 21 km (13 mi) long.

The restored Centro Histórico, with its plazas, theater and cathedral, is the cruise-day highlight. It sits a mile from the ship, inside the area the U.S. advisory allows.

ShrimpPacífico beerAguachilePescado zarandeadoBanda musicCliff diversEl FaroPulmonía taxisCarnavalSport fishing
History

From first peoples to now

Tap an era to expand it.

Before 1531Totorame and Xixime

Totorame people fish and farm the coast. The Xixime hold the mountains.

1531Conquest

Nuño de Guzmán's forces enter the region, bringing war and disease.

1600s–1700sWatching the sea

A thinly settled coast where galleons and pirates pass offshore.

1820s–1890sGerman merchants

Opened to trade after independence, the port becomes the Pacific gateway for Sierra mining.

1847–48U.S. occupation

U.S. forces hold the port during the Mexican-American War.

1859–1873State capital

Mazatlán governs Sinaloa.

1864French bombardment

During the French intervention.

1900Pacífico

German brewers found the beer that now ships worldwide.

1914Bombed from the air

One of the first aerial bombings in history, during the Revolution.

1950s–1970sResort town

Sport fishing, then the Golden Zone hotels. Pulmonías appear in the 1960s.

1990s–2000sOld town reborn

The Centro Histórico is restored and becomes the city's cultural heart.

2012Baluarte Bridge

The record-height bridge links Mazatlán to Durango.

Fun facts

22 things to know about Mazatlán

  1. Mazatlán is Nahuatl for 'place of deer'. That's why the island off the Golden Zone is Isla de Venados, Deer Island.
  2. Spanish settlement here dates to May 14, 1531, during Nuño de Guzmán's conquest of the northwest.
  3. German immigrants in the mid-1800s built it into a trading port supplying the gold and silver mines of the Sierra.
  4. Pacífico was founded in 1900 by three Germans: Jorge Claussen, Germán Evers and Emilio Radostits. The label shows a life ring and anchor over Cerro del Crestón, the hill under El Faro.
  5. Pacífico comes in 180 ml cuartitos, 350 ml medias and 950 ml ballenas, 'whales'. All are 4.4% ABV.
  6. Banda sinaloense, the big brass-band sound, grew out of Bavarian brass-band influence.
  7. It was the capital of Sinaloa from 1859 to 1873.
  8. U.S. forces occupied the port in 1847–48, and the French bombarded it in 1864.
  9. In 1914, during the Revolution, it was bombed from an airplane. It is often cited as the second city ever bombed from the air.
  10. Opera star Ángela Peralta died of yellow fever here in 1883, days after arriving. The theater bears her name.
12 more facts
  1. El Faro on Cerro del Crestón shines from about 157 m (515 ft) and is often called one of the highest lighthouses in the world.
  2. The Malecón runs about 21 km along the shore.
  3. Pulmonías, open-air golf-cart taxis, were invented here in the 1960s. The name means 'pneumonia', after the breeze.
  4. Cliff divers at Olas Altas dive into shallow surf for tips.
  5. Carnaval de Mazatlán dates to the late 1800s and is billed as Mexico's largest.
  6. It is Mexico's largest Pacific commercial fishing port, mainly shrimp and tuna.
  7. Aguachile, raw shrimp 'cooked' in lime and chile, is a Sinaloa invention.
  8. About 500,000 people live in the municipality, second in Sinaloa after the capital, Culiacán.
  9. The nearby Baluarte Bridge was the world's highest cable-stayed bridge when it opened in 2012, about 403 m above the canyon floor.
  10. The Gran Acuario Mazatlán opened in 2023 and is one of Mexico's largest aquariums.
  11. Isla de la Piedra, Stone Island, isn't an island. It's a peninsula across the harbor channel.
  12. The Golden Zone hotel strip grew up between the 1950s and the 1970s.
Practical

Know before you go ashore

Getting ashore

  • A free tram runs from the ship through the commercial port to the terminal gate.
  • From the gate, follow the painted blue line about 1 mile (15–20 min) to Plazuela Machado.
  • Pulmonías are cash only, so agree the price first. Expect opening offers around $20, or $30–50 for a 1–2 h tour.

Snorkeling & animals

  • This is the weakest snorkel port. Make it your town and food day.
  • The ship's Deer Island kayak tour includes modest snorkeling, but the island is outside the advisory's named zone.

Safety

  • Sinaloa is U.S. Level 4, Do not travel, for terrorism and crime. Cruise visitors are covered only in the historic center (from Avenida Gutiérrez Nájera to the ocean) and along the Malecón as far as Route 503.
  • Why: the Sinaloa Cartel split into warring factions in September 2024, after its co-founder Ismael 'El Mayo' Zambada ended up in U.S. custody. He says El Chapo's son lured him onto a plane to Texas. Since then Los Chapitos (El Chapo's sons) and Los Mayos (Zambada's faction) have fought for control of the state.
  • Two years in, state figures count about 3,700 homicides and about 4,000 people missing statewide, and roughly 7,000 businesses have closed. Most of the violence is in and around Culiacán, the state capital, about 200 km north.
  • Mazatlán has had spillover. After a spike in August 2026, the Navy sent more than 1,700 marines to the city. The U.S. Embassy has also warned of armed carjackings and roadblocks on Highway 15 between Culiacán and Mazatlán.
  • The historic center and Malecón are where the advisory lets U.S. government staff go, so that's the zone it carves out for cruise visitors. Deer Island, Stone Island, the Golden Zone and the Sierra towns aren't named. The ideas here stay inside the zone.
  • Some websites claim Sinaloa dropped to Level 3 in 2026. That's false. Recheck travel.state.gov the week you sail.

Land's End

By the numbers

At a glance

Overview

What it's known for

Land's End is the tip of the 1,250 km (775 mi) Baja peninsula. The Pacific meets the Sea of Cortez at El Arco, the granite arch. San José del Cabo lies about 30 km east along the resort Corridor, and the two towns together form the municipality of Los Cabos.

You anchor in the bay and take a tender into the marina, right in town. It's a short day, so pick one water activity and one food stop.

El ArcoLover's BeachMarlin fishingHumpback whalesSea lionsFish tacosDamianaMarina nightlifeDesert golf
History

From first peoples to now

Tap an era to expand it.

10,000+ yrsThe Pericú

Hunter-fishers live on the cape. They call it Yenekamú.

1535–1542Spanish explorers

Cortés at La Paz (1535), Ulloa names the sea (1539), Cabrillo stops on his way north (1542).

1565–1815Galleon route

Manila galleons make landfall here after crossing the Pacific.

1587Cavendish

The English privateer captures the Santa Ana off the cape.

1709Woodes Rogers

A second galleon taken, with Robinson Crusoe's model aboard the raider.

1730–1734Missions and revolt

Mission San José del Cabo, then the Pericú revolt.

1900sCannery village

A small tuna-canning settlement.

1950sFly-in anglers

Private planes bring marlin fishermen and movie stars.

1973The highway

The Transpeninsular Highway finally reaches the cape.

1980s–nowLos Cabos

Planned resort development, an international airport and a population boom.

Fun facts

23 things to know about Cabo San Lucas

  1. The Pericú lived here for perhaps 10,000 years or more, fishing from rafts and hunting with the atlatl, a spear-thrower. They had died out by the late 1700s.
  2. Hernán Cortés came looking for pearls near La Paz in 1535 and was driven off.
  3. Francisco de Ulloa named the Sea of Cortés in 1539.
  4. Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo stopped here in 1542 on the way north to San Diego.
  5. From 1565 to 1815, Manila galleons sailed past carrying silk, porcelain and spices, with crews weak from scurvy after months at sea.
  6. In November 1587, 27-year-old Thomas Cavendish captured the galleon Santa Ana off the cape. He left about 190 survivors on the beach with the sails for tents.
  7. Woodes Rogers took another galleon here in 1709. Alexander Selkirk, the model for Robinson Crusoe, was aboard Rogers' ship.
  8. Only four Manila galleons were ever captured in 250 years. Two were taken in or near this bay.
  9. Jesuit Nicolás Tamaral founded Mission San José del Cabo in 1730 and was killed in the Pericú revolt of 1734.
  10. Into the mid-1900s it was a tiny tuna-cannery village.
13 more facts
  1. In the 1940s and 1950s, Hollywood stars and anglers flew in by private plane because there was no road.
  2. The Transpeninsular Highway was finished only in 1973. The government tourism developer FONATUR then built the resort zone.
  3. About 350,000 people live in Los Cabos today, up from a few thousand in the 1970s.
  4. Lover's Beach faces the calm bay. Divorce Beach, a few steps across the sand, faces the Pacific and has deadly surf. Don't swim there.
  5. Pelican Rock is a protected snorkel spot a short boat ride from the marina.
  6. A submarine canyon starts just offshore and drops past 1,000 m. Divers know it for its underwater 'sand falls'.
  7. Bisbee's Black & Blue marlin tournament pays out millions and is one of the richest fishing contests in the world.
  8. At Cabo Pulmo, about two hours away, fish biomass grew more than 400% after the reef was protected.
  9. Humpbacks breach off the arch from December to April. Gray whales calve in Baja's Pacific lagoons from January to March.
  10. Baja California Sur has only about 798,000 people, the second-smallest state population, but it is one of Mexico's fastest-growing states.
  11. Guerrero Negro, in the same state, has one of the world's largest saltworks, right beside the gray-whale lagoon you pass on the way down.
  12. Damiana liqueur comes in a bottle shaped like a goddess. Sammy Hagar opened Cabo Wabo Cantina in 1990.
  13. Geologists think the cape was once attached to mainland Mexico near Jalisco before the Gulf of California tore open.
Practical

Know before you go ashore

Getting ashore

  • Ships anchor near El Arco. The 10–20 minute tender ride lands inside Marina Cabo San Lucas, right in town.
  • Tender lines can run 15–45 minutes in the first two hours, and guests on ship tours board first.
  • Usable time is about 8 am to 1 pm. The last tender is likely 1:15–1:30 pm; confirm it in the daily program and be at the pier 45–60 minutes before it.
  • Water taxis to the arch and Lover's Beach run about $15–25 round trip. Uber is about $5–10 in town; taxis $15–20 and up.

Snorkeling & animals

  • Bring your masks. Take a water taxi to Lover's Beach and snorkel the bay-side rocks toward Pelican Rock.
  • Santa María and Chileno bays (20–25 min by car) are clearer, protected coves with lots of fish, but watch the clock.
  • Animal encounters: the ship sells dolphin and sea-lion encounters in Puerto Vallarta, and Cabo has dolphin centers and beach horseback rides.

Safety

  • Baja California Sur is U.S. Level 2 with no specific restrictions.
  • Never swim at Divorce Beach or anywhere on the Pacific side.

New Year's Eve in Cabo

Cabo's big event is the midnight fireworks over Médano Beach, plus beach-club parties and fireworks cruises. You'll be at sea by then. Town is festive and busy from midday. Pick up 12 grapes to take aboard for your own countdown.

ESTADOS UNIDOS MEXICANOS · 32 STATES

Mexico briefing

Country numbers, the three states you visit, money, manners, New Year's traditions and Spanish for the week.

Country

Mexico by the numbers

~132 Mpeoplethe world's largest Spanish-speaking country
~$1.8 TGDP2025; ~$13,900 per person vs $88,600 in the U.S.
$664.8 Bexports2025 record, +7.6%
$872.8 BU.S.–Mexico goods trade2025; Mexico has been #1 U.S. partner since 2023
~80%of exports go to the U.S.
11.2 Mcruise passengers2025 record, 3,156 ship calls

What Mexico sells

  • Vehicles and parts. Transportation is about 40% of U.S.–Mexico trade.
  • Computers and data-center servers: computer processors alone were about $80.5 billion in 2025, and tech overtook autos as the top export sector.
  • Electrical machinery and crude oil.
  • Farm goods, $45.7 billion; the U.S. buys about 89%.
  • Beer (Mexico is the world's top exporter), avocados and tequila.
States

Where your three states rank

Safety

U.S. travel advisory by state

Mexico overallLevel 2

Reasons listed: terrorism, crime and kidnapping. Violent crime (homicide, kidnapping, carjacking, robbery) happens in many parts of the country. U.S. government staff must use dispatched taxis or ride apps and can't drive between cities after dark.

Jalisco · Puerto VallartaLevel 3

Terrorism, crime and kidnapping. Jalisco is the CJNG cartel's home state; gang battles have reached tourist areas of Guadalajara, and U.S. citizens have been kidnapped. No restrictions in Puerto Vallarta itself.

Sinaloa · MazatlánLevel 4

Terrorism and crime. An internal Sinaloa Cartel war since September 2024 has left about 3,700 people dead and 4,000 missing statewide. Cruise visitors: historic center and Malecón only.

Baja California Sur · CaboLevel 2

Terrorism and crime. No specific restrictions for travel anywhere in the state.

Why the levels are what they are

Why 'terrorism'?
In February 2025 the U.S. designated the Sinaloa Cartel, the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) and several other cartels as Foreign Terrorist Organizations. Since then 'terrorism' appears in the advisory wording for most of Mexico.
What the levels mean
Level 1 is normal precautions and Level 4 is do not travel. The restrictions under each state are the rules for U.S. government employees, which the State Department suggests visitors follow.
Why Sinaloa is Level 4
Since Sept 9, 2024, two Sinaloa Cartel factions, Los Chapitos and Los Mayos, have been at war. It began after co-founder Ismael 'El Mayo' Zambada was flown to Texas and arrested; he says El Chapo's son kidnapped him. Most violence is in and around Culiacán.
Jalisco's big day in 2026
On Feb 22, 2026, the army killed CJNG leader 'El Mencho'. For several hours cartel members burned vehicles at roadblocks across Jalisco, smoke rose over Puerto Vallarta, and some flights were canceled. Things largely returned to normal the next day.

If something flares up while you're ashore

  • Burning vehicles or roadblocks (narcobloqueos) are aimed at police and soldiers. Go indoors, to a hotel, restaurant or shop, and wait rather than trying to get past.
  • The ship is the safest place to be. Head back once roads are clear, and tell the ship if you'll be late; the port agent's number is in the daily program.
  • Call 911 for emergencies; it works in Mexico.
  • Before you go, enroll in the State Department's STEP program to get alerts, and save the U.S. consular agency contacts for Puerto Vallarta, Mazatlán and Los Cabos from travel.state.gov.
  • Keep phones charged and share your location within the group while ashore.

Advisory as reissued May 29, 2026; figures from Sinaloa state data reported in September 2026. Recheck travel.state.gov the week before you sail.

Manners & money

Etiquette and tipping

  • Say 'Buenos días' or 'Buenas tardes' before asking anything. It changes how people respond.
  • Haggle only at markets, and keep it friendly.
  • Dress modestly in churches.
  • Drink bottled or purified water.
  • Pay in pesos. It's almost always cheaper than paying in dollars.

Tipping

Restaurants
10–15% (check whether 'servicio' is already on the bill)
Guides
About $5–10 per person
Porters
20–50 pesos
Pulmonía or taxi
Not expected; round up

The poinsettia is native to Mexico, and it's named for Christmas Eve. Nativity scenes stay up through Jan 6.

Mexico's April Fools' Day. It falls on your second sea day.

One grape and one wish for each chime.

Red for love, yellow for money.
The empty suitcase
Walk around the block with an empty suitcase for a year of travel. A lap of the promenade deck counts.

For prosperity.

Rosca de reyes, a ring-shaped sweet bread, is already in bakeries when you visit.

Field guide

Which whale is that?

Checklist

Wildlife you might see

Tick what you spot. It saves on this phone.

Gray whale

Eschrichtius robustus
Dec–AprGood on sea days

Where: Off Baja's Pacific coast, heading south to the lagoons

ID: Low, heart- or V-shaped blow. No dorsal fin, just a row of 'knuckles' along the back. Mottled gray with white barnacle patches.

13–15 m long, about 36 tonnes. Their 10,000-mile round trip between the Arctic and Baja is one of the longest migrations of any mammal.

Humpback whale

Megaptera novaeangliae
Dec–MarVery good in PV and Cabo

Where: Banderas Bay and off Land's End

ID: Bushy blow about 3 m tall. Small dorsal fin on a hump. Very long white flippers. Shows its tail flukes before a deep dive and often breaches.

The pattern under each tail fluke is unique, like a fingerprint. Researchers identify individuals from photos of them.

Blue whale

Balaenoptera musculus
Mostly Jan–AprRare in December

Where: Gulf of California and offshore Baja

ID: Very tall, straight column blow up to 9 m. Long, mottled blue-gray back. A tiny dorsal fin far back, seen only as it rolls.

The largest animal that has ever lived. Its heart is about the size of a small car.

Fin whale

Balaenoptera physalus
Year-roundPossible near the Gulf mouth

Where: Sea of Cortez, which has a resident population

ID: Tall column blow. A curved dorsal fin appears soon after the blow. The lower jaw is white on the right side only.

One of the fastest whales, able to sprint at about 20 knots, faster than your ship's average.

Common dolphin

Delphinus spp.
Year-roundGood

Where: Open water all along the route

ID: Big, splashy pods. A yellow-and-gray hourglass pattern on the side. Often rides the bow wave.

Pods can number in the hundreds or even thousands.

Bottlenose dolphin

Tursiops truncatus
Year-roundGood near ports

Where: Bays and harbors

ID: Uniform gray, short stubby beak, tall curved fin. Smaller groups than common dolphins.

Each has a signature whistle that works like a name.

California sea lion

Zalophus californianus
Year-roundNear-certain in Cabo

Where: Rocks at Land's End, La Jolla Cove, San Diego Bay buoys

ID: Visible ear flaps. Walks on its big front flippers. Loud barking.

Males can reach about 350 kg, three to four times the size of females.

Harbor seal

Phoca vitulina
Pupping Dec–MayGood from the seawall

Where: Children's Pool, La Jolla

ID: No ear flaps. Spotted coat. Wriggles on its belly instead of walking.

The beach closes to people every Dec 15 – May 15 so the seals can pup.

Brown pelican

Pelecanus occidentalis
Year-roundCertain

Where: Every port

ID: Big gray-brown bird with a huge pouched bill. Flies in lines low over the water, then plunge-dives headfirst.

Air sacs under the skin cushion the impact of its dives.

Magnificent frigatebird

Fregata magnificens
Year-roundVery good

Where: Soaring over every Mexican port

ID: Black, with long angular M-shaped wings and a deep forked tail. Hangs motionless high above the harbor.

It can't swim or take off from water. It steals fish from other birds in flight and can stay aloft for weeks.

Blue-footed booby

Sula nebouxii
Year-roundGood on a Marietas trip

Where: Islas Marietas

ID: Brown-and-white seabird with unmistakable bright blue feet.

Males show off their feet in a high-stepping courtship dance. Bluer feet signal a healthier mate.

Mobula ray

Mobula munkiana
Mostly springLucky

Where: Sea of Cortez

ID: Small rays that leap clear of the water and belly-flop, often several at once.

Nobody is quite sure why they jump. Ideas include courtship, communication and shaking off parasites.

Olive ridley sea turtle

Lepidochelys olivacea
Nesting tails off in DecPossible snorkeling

Where: PV beaches and Los Arcos

ID: Small, olive-green turtle with a heart-shaped shell.

They nest in mass arrivals called arribadas, sometimes thousands of females at once.

Garibaldi

Hypsypops rubicundus
Year-roundCertain if you snorkel

Where: La Jolla Cove

ID: Bright solid orange fish in the kelp. Impossible to miss.

California's state marine fish. It's protected, so no taking them.

Card games

Rules for a standard deck

Tap a game for the rules. These are the common versions; agree on house rules before you start.

HeartsTrick-taking3–6 players, best with 4

Have the lowest score when someone reaches 100. Avoid hearts (1 point each) and the queen of spades (13).

Setup
Deal all 52 cards, 13 each. Before play, pass three cards: left on hand 1, right on hand 2, across on hand 3, no pass on hand 4, then repeat.
Play
  • Whoever holds the 2♣ leads it.
  • Follow suit if you can. If you can't, play anything.
  • Highest card of the suit led wins the trick, and the winner leads next.
  • You can't lead hearts until a heart has been played on a trick (hearts are 'broken'), unless you have nothing else.
  • Common house rule: no hearts or queen of spades on the first trick.
Scoring
Each heart taken is 1 point; the Q♠ is 13. Take every heart and the Q♠ ('shoot the moon') and you score 0 while everyone else takes 26.

Pass high spades and high hearts early. Short on a suit? Empty it so you can dump points later. · About 45–60 min.

SpadesTrick-taking, bidding4 players, in pairs

First team to 500 points.

Setup
Partners sit across from each other. Deal all 52 cards, 13 each.
Play
  • Each player bids how many tricks they expect to win. Partners add their bids for the team's contract.
  • A bid of 'nil' means you promise to win zero tricks.
  • Spades are always trump. You can't lead spades until one has been played on a trick, unless you have only spades.
  • Follow suit if you can. If you can't, you may trump with a spade or throw anything.
  • Highest spade wins the trick; if no spade was played, the highest card of the suit led wins.
Scoring
Make your contract: 10 points per trick bid, plus 1 per extra trick ('bag'). Miss it: lose 10 per trick bid. Every 10 bags costs 100 points. Nil: +100 if you take no tricks, −100 if you take any.

Bid conservatively at first. Bags add up fast. · About 60 min.

Thirty-OneDraw and discard2–9 players

Hold three cards of one suit totaling as close to 31 as possible. Be the last player with lives left.

Setup
Everyone starts with three lives (coins or chips). Deal three cards each. Put the rest face down as the stock and turn the top card up to start the discard pile.
Play
  • Card values: ace 11, face cards 10, others their number. Only cards of one suit count toward your total.
  • On your turn, take the top card of the stock or the discard pile, then discard one card.
  • Instead of drawing, you can knock. Everyone else gets one more turn, then all hands are shown.
  • If you ever hold exactly 31, show it right away. Everyone else loses a life.
Scoring
After a showdown, the lowest hand loses a life (in many games, a knocker who is lowest loses two). Out of lives, you're out. Last player standing wins.

Common variant: three of a kind counts as 30½. · About 15–30 min.

EuchreTrick-taking4 players, in pairs

First team to 10 points.

Setup
Use only the 9, 10, J, Q, K and A of each suit (24 cards). Deal five each and turn the next card face up.
Play
  • Going around, each player can tell the dealer to pick up the face-up card (its suit becomes trump) or pass. The dealer then discards a card.
  • If all pass, go around again and anyone may name a different suit as trump, or pass.
  • In trump, the jack of trump (right bower) is highest, then the other jack of the same color (left bower), then A, K, Q, 10, 9.
  • Follow suit if you can. The left bower counts as a trump card, not its printed suit.
  • The team that chose trump needs at least 3 of the 5 tricks.
Scoring
Choosing team takes 3 or 4 tricks: 1 point. All 5: 2 points. Fewer than 3 ('euchred'): the other team gets 2. Play alone and take all 5: 4 points.

House rule 'stick the dealer': if everyone passes twice, the dealer must name trump. · About 30–45 min.

Crazy EightsShedding2–7 players

Be first to play all your cards.

Setup
Deal five cards each (seven with two players). Turn the top card of the stock face up to start the pile.
Play
  • Play a card that matches the top card's suit or rank.
  • Eights are wild: play one any time and name the next suit.
  • If you can't play, draw from the stock until you can.
Scoring
The winner scores the cards left in others' hands: 50 for each eight, 10 for face cards, number value for the rest. Play to an agreed total.

Save your eights for when you're stuck. · About 15 min.

SpoonsSpeed3–13 players

Don't be the one left without a spoon.

Setup
Put spoons in the middle, one fewer than the number of players. Deal four cards each.
Play
  • The dealer draws from the deck and passes a card to the left. Everyone keeps four cards, picking up from the right and passing left, all at once.
  • When you get four of a kind, quietly take a spoon.
  • As soon as anyone takes a spoon, everyone else may grab one too.
Scoring
The player without a spoon gets a letter: S, P, O, O, N. Spell SPOON and you're out.

No spoons aboard? Use sugar packets or napkins. · About 10 min.

Gin RummyDraw and discard2 players

Form your hand into sets and runs, and reach 100 points first.

Setup
Deal ten cards each. Put the rest face down and turn one card up to start the discard pile.
Play
  • On your turn, draw from the stock or the discard pile, then discard one card.
  • Sets are three or four cards of the same rank. Runs are three or more in a row of one suit (ace is low).
  • Unmatched cards are 'deadwood': face cards 10, aces 1, others their number.
  • Knock when your deadwood is 10 or less: lay down your hand and discard. Your opponent can add their loose cards to your sets and runs.
Scoring
Knocker scores the difference in deadwood. If the opponent's deadwood is equal or lower, they 'undercut' and score the difference plus 25. Going gin (no deadwood) scores the opponent's deadwood plus 25.

Watch the discard pile to learn what your opponent is collecting. · About 30 min.

PresidentShedding4–8 players

Get rid of your cards first and become President.

Setup
Deal out the whole deck. Cards rank 2 (high), A, K, Q down to 3 (low).
Play
  • The player with the 3♣ leads one card, or a pair, three or four of the same rank.
  • Each next player must play the same number of cards at a higher rank, or pass.
  • When everyone passes, the last player to play clears the pile and leads anything.
Scoring
First out is President, last is Scum. Next hand, Scum gives their two best cards to the President, who gives back any two.

Hold your 2s to take control of the lead late. · About 20–40 min.

Oh Hell!Trick-taking, bidding3–7 players

Win exactly the number of tricks you bid.

Setup
Round one deals 1 card each, round two deals 2, and so on as high as the deck allows, then back down. Turn the next card up for trump.
Play
  • Everyone bids how many tricks they'll take. The dealer, bidding last, may not make the total of all bids equal the number of tricks.
  • Follow suit if you can; otherwise trump or throw anything. Highest trump wins, else highest of the suit led.
Scoring
Hit your bid exactly: 10 points plus your bid. Miss by any amount: 0. Highest total after the last round wins.

In the one-card rounds, a bid of 0 is often the smart play. · About 45 min.

SpeedSpeed2 players

Be first to get rid of all your cards.

Setup
Put two cards face down in the middle and a face-down stack of five beside each. Split the remaining 40: each player takes 20, holds five as a hand and keeps 15 as a draw pile.
Play
  • Both players flip a middle card at the same time.
  • Play cards one higher or lower than either middle card, as fast as you can. Suits don't matter, and ace connects to both king and 2.
  • Refill your hand to five from your draw pile as you go.
  • If both players are stuck, flip new middle cards from the side stacks.
Scoring
First to empty their hand and draw pile wins.

No turns. Speed matters more than strategy. · About 5 min.

Egyptian RatscrewSpeed, slapping2–6 players

Win all the cards.

Setup
Deal the whole deck face down. Don't look at your cards.
Play
  • Take turns flipping your top card onto a central pile.
  • Slap the pile when two cards of the same rank land in a row (a double) or with one card between them (a sandwich). First to slap takes the pile.
  • When someone plays a face card or ace, the next player gets chances to play one too: 4 for an ace, 3 for a king, 2 for a queen, 1 for a jack. If they fail, the player who played the face card takes the pile.
Scoring
A wrong slap costs you a card to the bottom of the pile. Run out of cards and you can still slap your way back in.

Keep your rings off. It gets physical. · About 20 min.

How to carry it

Put it on your home screen

  1. On your iPhone, open daniel-beachy.github.io/cruise-guide-v1 in Safari while you have a connection.
